ch11.anchor: Four of the five were put to death.
ch11.note: The five were seized on 24 August 1929 and Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, and Xing Shizhen were shot at Longhua on 30 August; only Zhang Jichun survived. The betrayer was Bai Xin, Peng Pai's own secretary, whom the Red Squad hunted down and killed that November (the subject of the next chapter). Corroborated by independent scholarship. Peng Pai, Yang Yin, and Bai Xin are noted at their first appearances in chapters 2 and 4.

The work-study movement carried some 1,600 Chinese students to France between 1919 and 1921 to study while laboring in factories; many, radicalized there, went on to lead the CCP. In September 1921 a group protesting the new Franco-Chinese University of Lyon's refusal to admit them occupied the campus, and the French authorities deported 104 of them—Yan Changyi and the future Party leaders Cai Hesen and Li Lisan among them. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: the Guangzhou Uprising he was named
ch11.note: The Guangzhou (Canton) Uprising of 11–13 December 1927, a Communist rising that briefly proclaimed the short-lived Guangzhou Soviet, or Canton Commune, before being crushed with heavy loss of life. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: and launched and led the Canton
ch11.note: The Canton–Hong Kong Strike (June 1925 to October 1926), a sixteen-month general strike and boycott against British and Japanese interests, one of the largest labor actions of the period, touched off by the May Thirtieth killings. Corroborated.

The C.C. Clique, a powerful right-wing faction of the Kuomintang led by the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which controlled the party's organization apparatus and much of its secret-police and anti-Communist work. Chen Lifu, named just below, was its co-chief. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: Hearing the Way in the morning, one may die content at evening
ch11.note: A saying of Confucius, Analects IV.8 (朝闻道，夕死可瞻): if in the morning one hears the Way, one may die content that evening. Yang Yin quotes it as a scholar's calm in the face of death; Zhou Enlai's memorial circular, at the chapter's end, quotes the same line.

So Zhou Enlai's contemporary account has it—that on the night of 28 August 1929 an attempt was made on Chiang Kai-shek's life in Shanghai, throwing the garrison into a panic that hastened the martyrs' execution. The incident is not readily corroborated in independent sources and is given here as the source states it.

ch11.anchor: from Xiong Shihui at the top
ch11.note: Xiong Shihui (1893–1974), Kuomintang general and Songhu (Shanghai–Songjiang) Garrison Commander from September 1928 to 1930, later governor of Jiangxi and a leading figure of the Political Study Clique. That the order to shoot the five came down through his command is corroborated (Baidu Baike; Chinese Wikipedia).

ch11.anchor: How the Four Comrades Peng, Yang, Yan, and Xing Were Seized and Killed by the Enemy
ch11.note: Author's note. The essay appeared in the CCP central organ the Red Flag Daily on 13 August 1930.

ch11.anchor: Ke Lin, who knew Bai Xin's history well, has said
ch11.note: Author's note. Ke Lin, Recollections of Peng Pai (Renmin Chubanshe, 1992), pp. 214–215. Ke Lin himself is noted in chapter 4.

ch11.anchor: Li Qiang, who was on the scene that day and helped direct the operation
ch11.note: Author's note. "Bright as Frost the Naked Blade Before the Steps: How the Central Special Section Tried to Rescue Peng Pai and Punish the Traitors," Zhonghua Yinglie (Chinese Martyrs), 1986, no. 5.

ch12.note: Peng Shilu (1925–2021), Peng Pai's son, orphaned by his father's execution and raised in hiding, became the first chief designer of China's nuclear submarines and the "father of China's naval nuclear propulsion," and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; The Paper).

ch12.anchor: the residence of Fan Zhengbo on Avenue Joffre (today Central Huaihai Road)
ch12.note: Avenue Joffre (霞飞路, today Central Huaihai Road) was the main boulevard of the French Concession and a fashionable Shanghai district; its cross-streets and lanes give both parts of this chapter their name. Rue Bourgeat (藆石路), onto which the lane's other end opened, is today Changle Road.
Author's note. Shi Bao (The Eastern Times), 13 November 1929. The bracketed cross-references within the quotation, noting where the report contradicts itself, are the newspaper's own or the author's.

ch12.anchor: chief of the detective bureau of the Songhu Gendarmerie Command at Longhua and head of the anti-Communist headquarters for the Chinese city of Shanghai
ch12.note: The North China Daily News, which the book reproduces in Chinese translation, overstates Bai Xin's rank here; he had been secretary of the CCP Central Military Commission and, after informing, a protege of the Kuomintang's Shanghai party branch, not the head of a garrison detective bureau. The paper's account otherwise squares closely with the Chinese versions of the killing, down to the address and the hired car.

ch12.anchor: On 9 November the Kuomintang-run Shanghai Minguo Ribao
ch12.note: The date as the source prints it. The report reproaches the Concession for failing to prevent or solve the killing, yet is dated 9 November—two days before Bai Xin was shot on the 11th. The discrepancy, most likely a misprint for a later date, is left as printed.

The claim that the American intelligence service sent an agent named Ross whose own confidant fed information to the CCP for a monthly stipend rests on the Party's memoir literature and is not independently corroborated.

ch12.anchor: with Kang Sheng holding the post of Third Section chief
ch12.note: Kang Sheng (noted in chapter 9), who here briefly oversees the Special Section's Third Section, later became the head of the Party's security and intelligence apparatus and a principal persecutor in the Yan'an Rectification and the Cultural Revolution. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: when I was writing General Chen Geng
ch12.note: General Chen Geng (陈赋大将) is Mu Xin's own earlier book. The exchange that follows—over whether Tan Zhongyu's surname was Tan or Dan—is the author recounting his research correspondence with Li Qiang, and is reproduced as he set it down.
